extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, PTAB practitioners, appellate counsel, and patent prosecutors involved in IPR appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal criteria for evaluating Patent Trial and Appeal Board decisions on anticipation/obviousness, claim construction, petition scope, and standards of review on appeal to the Federal Circuit. Focuses on how prior art is read, what issues are fairly presented in a petition, and applicable appellate standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition scope defines litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The petitioner’s contentions . . . define the scope of the litigation all the way from institution through to conclusion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Board deems a claim unpatentable on a ground absent from the petition, that can be error. Courts examine whether the Board's final written decision stayed within the grounds and arguments actually presented in the petition (examples: SAS Inst., Koninklijke Philips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewability of institution decisions (35 U.S.C. § 314(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: “The determination by the Director whether to institute an inter partes review under this section shall be final and nonappealable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 314(d) bars review of decisions closely related to institution, but it does not prevent examining whether the final written decision stayed within the petition's confines. The court distinguishes between undoing institution and ensuring the final decision proceeds according to law (citing Thryv, SAS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse-of-discretion for what is fairly presented in a petition
rubrics_metrics.description: “We review the Board’s judgments concerning what arguments are fairly presented in a petition and other pleadings for abuse of discretion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions about whether the petition fairly presented particular grounds or arguments are reviewed for abuse of discretion (Netflix, Corephotonics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of review for obviousness and facts
rubrics_metrics.description: “We review the Board’s obviousness determinations de novo and its factual findings underlying those determinations for substantial evidence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal conclusion of obviousness is reviewed de novo; underlying factual findings (what a prior art reference discloses, motivation to combine, etc.) are reviewed for substantial evidence (In re Hodges; Mettler-Toledo cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation is a question of fact from the skilled artisan perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: “What a prior art reference discloses is a question of fact.” and “Anticipation is an inquiry viewed from the perspective of one skilled in the art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a reference anticipates a claim limitation depends on what a skilled artisan would understand from the reference (Mettler-Toledo, Wasica). The Federal Circuit will defer to substantial-evidence-supported factual findings about disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert testimony to interpret prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: “Expert testimony may shed light on what a skilled artisan would reasonably understand or infer from a prior art reference.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert evidence is appropriate to explain how a skilled artisan would read a prior-art disclosure and to support inferences about what the reference discloses (Acoustic Tech.; cited supporting authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board may err by relying on grounds not presented in the petition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board cannot rely on a theory of unpatentability that was not advanced in the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent (e.g., Koninklijke) shows the Board abuses its discretion if it bases an unpatentability finding on a combination or theory not raised in the petition. Courts will reverse where the final decision departs from the petition's grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — 'protected resources' (Board's adopted definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Board's construction: “[A]n application, an object, a document, a page, a file, executable code, or other computational resource, communication-type resource, etc., identified by a Uniform Resource Locator (URL), or more generally, a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI), that can only be accessed by an authenticated and/or authorized user.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specific construction was used to assess whether a prior-art reference disclosed ‘protected resources’; the construction can be outcome-determinative for anticipation/obviousness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — 'identifier associated with the user' (Board's adopted definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Board's construction: “information that uniquely identifies the user.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction guided whether Sunada’s ‘User ID’ qualified as the claimed identifier and whether the prior art taught transmitting that identifier to the second system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between anticipation and obviousness when a reference 'suggests' a teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of terms like 'suggests' or 'strongly suggests' often arises in §103 obviousness inquiries, but can appear when explaining how a skilled artisan would read an express teaching in the context of anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may explain that an express statement in the reference (e.g., ‘web application’) would lead a skilled artisan to understand an implicit detail (e.g., use of URLs) without performing a §103 modification. The Board must not be deemed to be impermissibly modifying prior art when it is instead drawing reasonable inferences about what the reference discloses to a skilled artisan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence standard and reasonable-inference principle
rubrics_metrics.description: “A finding is supported by substantial evidence if a reasonable mind might accept the evidence to support the finding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts accept inferences the Board reasonably draws from the record (Quake v. Lo; Redline Detection). Substantial-evidence review asks whether a reasonable factfinder could reach the Board's conclusion based on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of abandonment/concession at oral hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: If a petitioner abandons a ground (for example, concedes an anticipation challenge at oral hearing), the Board may find that ground not proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petitioner’s concession or abandonment can eliminate a ground from consideration; the Board’s later analysis must reflect which grounds remain actively pursued (illustrated by Rakuten abandoning its §102 ground).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferences about conventional technology usage (e.g., URLs for web applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: A skilled artisan may be assumed to understand conventional aspects of technology (e.g., that web pages are identified by URLs or URIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reference refers to commonplace technology (like ‘web application’), the Board may reasonably infer conventional attributes (such as URL usage) based on the record and expert acknowledgment that such usage was conventional at the priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in claim-to-prior-art mapping for corresponding circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a claim limitation is taught by a prior art reference, the prior art must disclose the limitation in the same circumstance recited by the claim (e.g., requesting user attributes from the first system 'in response to a determination' that the second system lacks sufficient information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two claims that are textually similar can be differently patentable depending on the exact actor and circumstance claimed (example: sending a request to the first system vs. sending to the fourth system); the Board must find the prior art discloses the same temporal/causal circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness rules for appeals and cross‑appeals from PTAB decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of appeal to the Director must be filed no later than sixty‑three days after the date of the final Board decision; if one party timely files, other parties may file within 14 days after the first notice (Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late notices can be cured by a retroactive extension upon a showing of excusable neglect under 37 C.F.R. § 90.3(c)(ii); parties should address timeliness issues early in proceedings.
